Hydrogem Atom Abstraction
Copper-Catalyzed Radical Allene C(sp
2
) � H Cyanation
Youhao Wei
+
, Zheng Wang
+
, Kaifeng Wang
+
, Jiang-Kai Qiu,* Zhaoshan Wang, Haotian Li,
Xiu Duan, Kai Guo, Xiaoguang Bao,* and Xinxin Wu*
Dedicated to Professor Kendall N. Houk on the occasion of his 80th birthday
Abstract: While the hydrogen atom abstraction (HAA)
from C(sp
3
) � H bond has been well explored, the
radical-mediated chemo- and regio-selective functionali-
zation of allenic C(sp
2
) � H bond via direct HAA from
C(sp
2
) � H bond of allene remains an unsolved challenge
in synthetic chemistry. This is primarily due to inherent
challenges with addition of radical intermediates to
allenes, regioselectivity of HAA process, instability of
allenyl radical toward propargyl radical et al. Herein, we
report a copper catalyzed allenic C(sp
2
) � H cyanation of
an array of tri- and di-substituted allenes with excep-
tional site-selectivity, while mono-substituted allene was
successfully cyanated, albeit with a low yield. In the
developed strategy, steric N-fluoro-N-alkylsulfonamide,
serving as precursor of hydrogen atom abstractor, plays
a crucial role in achieving the desired regioselectivity
and avoiding addition of N-centered radical to allene.
D irect insertion of a functional group into a molecule via
C � H bond functionalization represents one of most inves-
tigated approaches in organic synthetic chemistry. Because
of the ubiquity of C � H bonds in organic molecules, by
providing access to the desired product with improved atom
and step economy over classical synthetic methods, C � H
bond functionalization is a particularly powerful toolbox in
terms of synthetic efficiency especially when applied to
medicinal chemistry, synthesis of natural products and
bioactive compounds.
[1–3]
To address this challenging task,
one of the most appealing concepts, which involves the
homolytic cleavage of the C � H bond via hydrogen atom
abstraction (HAA) procedure, has been successfully
devised.
[4–10]
Tremendous progress has been made for
aliphatic C(sp
3
) � H bond functionalization via radical HAA
process. Nevertheless, allenes are notably absent on the list
of suitable substrates as hydrogen donors that have been
reported (Figure 1A).
[11]
In radical reactions, allenes are
especially reactive due to unique twisted orthogonal π
system that is prone to undergo radical addition to C = C
bond.
[12]
Additionally, to realize allene C � H functionaliza-
tion, several challenging issues should be addressed: (1)
Given that both allenyl and alkenyl C � H bond are sp
2
hybrid, is allenyl C � H bond similar to alkenyl C � H bond,
which has so high bond dissociation energy (BDE) that the
cleavage of allenyl C � H bond is not easy to access?
[13]
(2) In
the presence of both allenyl C � H bond and other reactive
C(sp
3
) � H bonds, how could we control the site-selectivity
during HAA process? (3) Due to the resonance between

allenyl radical and propargyl radical,
[14]
how could we rise to
the challenge of selectively trapping allenyl radical? Accord-
ingly, direct radical C � H functionalization of allenes is
unknown, although one example of radical allene function-
alization via radical addition followed by β-hydride elimi-
nation has been reported by Zhang and co-workers.
[15]
Some formal functionalizations of allene C � H bond have
been reported via sequential C = C addition/C � H cleavage or
concerted C = C activation/C � H deprotonation followed by
S
E
2’.
[16–20]
They are mechanistically distinct from catalytic
allene C � H activation which has been elegantly disclosed by
Carreira et al.
[21]
(Figure 2A) Hou and co-workers also
reported rare-earth-catalyzed allene C � H activation to
synthesize cyclopropane and cyclopropenes (Figure 2B).
[22]
Additionally, radical transformations for allene synthesis
have been elegantly realized through radical 1,4-addition to
1,3-enynes,
[23]
transformations from propargylic
compounds,
[24]
1,2-elimination
[25]
et al. Despite of these
processes, direct C � H functionalization of easily available
allenes without the requirement of direction-group and with
broader substrate scope in atom- and step-economic mode is
very attractive and highly desired. To the best of our
knowledge, no related works have been reported to date.
Stimulated by the enormous progress of radical HAA
chemistry and copper-catalyzed system using N-fluoro-
arylsulfonamides elegantly developed by the Liu group,
[26]
we hypothesized that allenyl radical could be produced
through a hydrogen atom abstraction process mediated by
bulky radical species that hardly adds to allene owing to
steric hinderance.
[27]
By utilizing copper salt as catalyst and
N-fluoro-N-alkylsulfonamide as HAA reagent, direct cyana-
tion of allene C � H bonds under mild conditions were
achieved with good yields and exclusive selectivities (Fig-
ure 1B).
Trisubstituted allene (1 a) with an allenyl C � H bond and
two formal allyl C � H bonds that might compete in HAA
process, was subjected to screening of the reaction parame-
ters. Mechanistically, the interaction of a Cu salt/ligand with
an HAA reagent, N-fluoro-N-alkylamide, generated a N-
centered radical that could abstract hydrogen atom from
allene C � H bond to give allenyl radical. Interaction between
allenyl radical and LCuCN species would afford cyanated
product (2 a) via reductive elimination of Cu(III) complex.
Based on the assumption that the HAA reagent should be
capable of regioselective HAA and could also avoid
addition to allene, initial experiment was started from
screening HAA reagents with the use of CuOAc as catalyst
and 4,4’-di-tert-butyl-2,2’-dipyridyl (dtbbpy, L1) as ligand.
Although CF
3
-substituted benzamide failed to provide
corresponding product (A1, Table 1, entry 1), the reaction
using sulfonylamide (A2) proceeded smoothly to give
desired product (2 a) with moderate yield and perfect
regioselectivity (Table 1, entry 2). Notably, no allyl C � H
cyanated product was found. To increase the steric hin-
drance of N-centered radical to avoid its addition to allene,
ortho-trifluoro sulfonylamide (A3) was synthesized and
subjected to this condition (Table 1, entry 3). However, a
decreasing yield was provided. Instead, ortho-chloro sulfo-
nylamide (A5) gave the best yield (Table 1, entry 5). Either

decreasing or increasing steric hindrance was detrimental to
the reaction outcome (Table 1, entries 4 and 6). The use of
other ligands such as bathocuproine (L2), 2,2’ : 6’,2’’-terpyr-
idine (L3) and bis((3aR,8aS)-8,8a-dihydro-3aH-indeno[1,2-
d]oxazol-2-yl)methane (L4) resulted in poor yields (Table 1,
entries 7–9).
The optimized reaction condition for regioselective
allene C � H cyanation was used in an investigation of the
generality of our protocol. First, the scope of trisubstituted
allene was examined (Figure 3). Allene (1 b) with a long
pendent aliphatic chain was also suitable for the reaction to
provide corresponding cyanated product (2 b). A portfolio
of allenes bearing either electron-donating or -withdrawing
aryls were found to be suitable substrates, leading to the
products (2 c–2 h) in moderate to excellent yields and good
regioselectivities. In addition to the phenyl ring, the
naphthyl and pyridyl allenes were also well-tolerated,
resulting in the formation of corresponding products (2 i–2 j)
in synthetically useful yields. In lieu of methyl group, allenes
with the ethyl, benzyl, cyclopropyl and tetrahydronaphthyl
group were readily converted to desired cyanated com-
pounds (2 k–2 n). It is noteworthy that the presence of
benzylic C � H bonds (2 l) with low BDE had no effect on the
site-selective hydrogen abstraction from allenic C � H bond.
In terms of the example of 2 m, “radical clock” process-
driven ring-opening product derived from propargylic radi-
cal, a resonance structure of allenic radical, was not
detected. 1,1-Biaryl allenes were also compatible to yield the
desired products (2 o and 2 p). Remarkably, successful
conversion of 1 p derived from Fenofibrate for the treatment
of hyperlipidemia, showcased the potential for application
of this protocol in late-stage elaboration of bioactive
compounds or drugs. Many structural units, such as ester
(2 q–2 v), chloride (2 s), and ketone (2 t) derived from
Loxoprofen, were well tolerated in this protocol. Especially,
some reactive C(sp
3
) � H bonds, including phenyl ether (2 w),
unprotected alcohol (2 x), and cyclic tertiary C(sp
3
) � H bond
(2 y) were intact under this condition. Of note, allenic C � H
bond (1 z) adjacent to cyclopropyl ring was readily cyanated
and no ring-opening product via “radical clock” process was
formed. The reaction with 1,3-diaryl allene gave desired
product (2 aa) successfully, albeit with a decreasing yield
probably attributing to high steric hinderance. In addition to
aryl-substituted allenes, allene substrates with alkyl groups
or complex molecular skeleton, were subjected to our

with excellent regioselectivities and moderate yields.
The compatibility of di- and mono-substituted allenes
with two or three allenic C � H bonds that might compete in
HAA process (Figure 3, bottom) were explored next.
Disubstituted allenes pedant with ortho-, meta-, and para-
halogenated aryl group smoothly underwent site-specific
HAA from allenyl C � H bonds near aliphatic chain with less
steric hinderance, leading to a set of trisubstituted allenes
(2 ad–2 ag) with synthetically useful yields and excellent
regioselectivities. Naphthyl and biphenyl allenes (1 ah–1 ai)
were found to be suitable substrates giving rise to the
desired products. In the case of 1,1-arylalkyl allene, the
abstraction of allenic C � H bond also proceeded readily to
furnish cyanated allene (2 aj). Interestingly, when using
monosubstituted allene (1 ai), the exclusive regioselectivity
of the HAA process occurred at terminal C � H bond instead
of benzyl C � H bond. However, a decreasing yield was given,
probably owing to addition of N-centered radical from
HAA reagent (A5) to allene leading to byproduct.
The scaled-up preparation of 1 a proceeded readily and
delivered a comparable yield, showing the practicality of the
protocol (Figure 4A). The products can be conveniently
transformed into other valuable compounds (Figure 4B).
For example, the allene in 2 a was converted to a tetra-
substituted alkene (3) by nucleophilic addition with p-
toluenethiol. Treating the allene with N-iodosuccinimide
(NIS) generated iodo-1,3-diene (4) through C � H bond
elimination. Similar elimination occurred when 2 a was then
subjected to the Suzuki coupling with 4-tolylboronic acid to
afford biaryldiene (5). The cyano group in 2 a could be
substituted with transformable functional units, such as
amide (6) or aldehyde (7), which offer a platform for further
elaborations. Deuteration of allenyl C � H of 2 ad with D

tion of allenyl C � H bond (Figure 5). The reactions with di-
and tri-substituted allenes (1 a, 1 y, 1 ad and 1 af) gave

Radical trapping experiment was carried out to probe
the radical species involved in the reaction (Figure 6A). In
the presence of TEMPO, the allene C � H cyanation was
inhibited and N-centered radical generated in situ was
successfully captured by TEMPO to give 8 that was detected
by HRMS. Furthermore, a radical-clock experiment was
designed to detect allenyl radical (Figure 6B), and desired
ring-opening product (10) was afforded. These results
confirmed the formation of N-centered radical and allenyl
radical in the transformation. The measured product isotope
effect of 2.3 for the KIE experiment of reactions with 1 c
and 1 c–d suggests that the intermolecular HAA process
might be the rate-limiting step in this process (Figure 6C).
To obtain a deeper understanding of chemo- and
regioselectivity of the cyanation of allenyl C(sp
2
) � H bond,
density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried
out (Figure 7). For the example of 1 a with an allenyl
C(sp
2
) � H bond and two allylic C(sp
3
) � H bonds, the
activation energy (ΔG
¼6
) for HAA process involving these
C � H bonds and the ΔG of this step were calculated and
shown in Figure 7A, demonstrating that HAA from allenyl
C(sp
2
) � H bond requires the lowest activation energy
(8.6 kcal/mol) and is exergonic by � 29.9 kcal/mol. In
addition, to explore the regioselectivities of these reactions,
BDEs of C � H bonds of substrate 1 a, were calculated and
shown in Figure 7B. These results illustrate that allenyl
C(sp
2
) � H bonds with lower BDE, are prone to be readily
cyanated through HAA process with relatively lower
activation barrier and more exergonic energy. Of note, BDE
of allenyl C(sp
2
) � H
b
bond is even lower than that of some
activated C(sp
3
) � H bonds, such as toluene (89.7 kcal/mol),
allylic C � H bond (about 88 kcal/mol), ethanol (95.9 kcal/
mol), tetrahydrofuran (THF, 92.1 kcal/mol) et al. This also
explains exclusive selectivity at the allenyl C(sp
2
) � H bond
even in the presence of some activated C(sp
3
) � H bonds.
Based on this study of the mechanism, a plausible
pathway is outlined in Figure 8. The interaction between
Cu(I) and the HAA reagent (A5) gives rise to a Cu(II)-
bound N-centered radical (A5-r). This radical (A5-r)
abstracts selectively a hydrogen atom from allene C � H bond
to provide the allenyl radical (INT1). The interaction
between Cu(II)F complex and TMSCN delivers a Cu(II)CN
species, which upon interception by INT1 furnishes INT2.
The ensuing reductive elimination of INT2 furnishes the
final product (2) and regenerates Cu(I) to perpetuate the
catalytic cycle.
In summary, a novel copper-catalyzed site-selective
radical allenyl C(sp
2
) � H functionalization has been de-
scribed. The key to the success of this reaction lies in the
regioselective intermolecular HAA process mediated by a
bulky HAA reagent, N-fluoro-N-alkylsulfonylamide, thus
avoiding its addition to allene. A set of valuable tetra-, tri-
and di-functionalized allene derivatives have been obtained
in synthetically useful yields in this way. DFT calculations
provide theoretical evidence supporting the regioselectivity
of this HAA process. The method features broad functional
group compatibility and high product diversity, and allows a
much broader chemical space for radical C(sp
2
) � H function-
alization.
